title: Device Fingerprinting Privacy Hardening Checklist
metaDescription: Comprehensive checklist to protect against device fingerprinting, canvas tracking, and invisible browser identification. Stop persistent tracking today.
intro: Device fingerprinting allows websites to identify you even after clearing cookies by analyzing your browser, screen, fonts, and hardware. This persistent tracking method is invisible and hard to detect, making it a serious privacy threat.

items.why: Standard browsers leak identifiable information through default settings and lack built-in fingerprint protection.
items.howTo: Use Firefox with privacy tweaks or Tor Browser. Avoid Chrome, Edge, and Safari for sensitive browsing.

items.task: Block scripts you don't need, with a blocker that can do it
items.why: JavaScript enables most fingerprinting techniques including canvas, WebGL, and audio fingerprinting.
items.howTo: In Firefox, install uBlock Origin, turn on advanced-user mode and use medium mode, allowing scripts site by site. Chrome's uBlock Origin Lite has no such mode, so switch browsers for this or use NoScript on Firefox.

items.why: Canvas fingerprinting creates unique images based on your graphics card and fonts to identify your device.
items.howTo: In Firefox, install the CanvasBlocker extension or set privacy.resistFingerprinting to true in about:config. Brave, Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser protect canvas readings by default.

items.why: WebGL reveals detailed graphics card information that creates a unique device signature.
items.howTo: Go to about:config in Firefox, set webgl.disabled to true. In Chrome, use flags or extensions to disable WebGL.

items.why: User-Agent reveals your exact browser version, OS, and device type, contributing to your fingerprint.
items.howTo: Keep your browser up to date so its user agent matches most other people's. Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser give everyone on the same operating system the same user agent. Avoid switcher extensions that set a rare value: a user agent that doesn't match your other signals makes you stand out.

items.why: Installed fonts create a unique signature since everyone has different font collections.
items.howTo: Use Firefox's resistFingerprinting setting or extensions that block font enumeration and provide standard fonts only.

items.why: This built-in feature spoofs many fingerprinting vectors including screen size, timezone, and hardware details.
items.howTo: Go to about:config, set privacy.resistFingerprinting to true. This may break some sites but significantly reduces fingerprinting.

items.why: Timezone reveals your geographic location and is combined with other data points for identification.
items.howTo: Firefox with privacy.resistFingerprinting, Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser report the same UTC time zone to every site. In other browsers, a time-zone extension can report UTC or a common time zone instead.

items.why: Unique screen resolutions and color depths help websites identify your specific device setup.
items.howTo: Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser use letterboxing, which rounds the window size sites see to a few common values; in Firefox, set privacy.resistFingerprinting.letterboxing to true for the same effect. Avoid resizing the window to unusual sizes.

items.why: CPU cores, memory, and graphics capabilities create unique device signatures.
items.howTo: Enable privacy.resistFingerprinting in Firefox or use specialized extensions that spoof navigator.hardwareConcurrency values.

items.why: Audio fingerprinting analyzes how your device processes sound to create unique acoustic signatures.
items.howTo: Install AudioContext Fingerprint Defender or use browsers with built-in audio fingerprint protection.

items.why: Battery level and charging status can be used for device identification and tracking.
items.howTo: Firefox and Safari don't give websites battery information. Chrome and Edge still do, so block the Battery Status API there with an extension.

items.why: You need to verify that your protection measures are working and your fingerprint isn't unique.
items.howTo: Visit Cover Your Tracks (the EFF's renamed Panopticlick), AmIUnique or BrowserLeaks monthly to test your fingerprint. Aim for a common, non-unique result.

items.why: Different activities require different privacy levels and using separate profiles prevents cross-contamination.
items.howTo: Create dedicated profiles for banking, social media, and general browsing with different fingerprint protection levels.

items.task: Use virtual machines for high-privacy activities
items.why: A VM keeps your real hardware details, fonts and files out of sight of the sites you visit.
items.howTo: Run your browser in a disposable VirtualBox or VMware VM and reset it to a clean snapshot after each session. A VM's virtual hardware can itself be rare, so use Tor Browser or Mullvad Browser inside it rather than a stock browser.

items.task: Use Tor Browser for maximum anonymity
items.why: Tor Browser provides the strongest fingerprint protection by making all users look identical.
items.howTo: Download official Tor Browser, never install extensions, don't maximize window, and avoid logging into personal accounts.

items.why: New fingerprinting techniques emerge constantly, requiring updated countermeasures and fresh configurations.
items.howTo: Update browsers, extensions, and test fingerprint monthly. Join privacy communities to stay informed about new threats.

pro_tips: Disable JavaScript completely for maximum protection - most fingerprinting requires JavaScript to function
Never use browser extensions in Tor Browser as they make you identifiable and defeat the anonymity
Test your setup with multiple fingerprinting sites as each tests different vectors and techniques
If this list is more setup than you want, Mullvad Browser and Tor Browser come with fingerprinting protection already configured, and Brave randomizes canvas, WebGL and audio readings by default
Reset your browser profile regularly to eliminate any accumulated tracking data or fingerprint evolution
